blocks.text: 1. Response Cache

blocks.alt: A query is checked against a response cache for whether it was already answered

blocks.text: Embedding Cache closed by placing its infrastructure choice separate from the main vector database. Response Cache, storing the complete generated answer for a given query and context is the second concrete application Caching pointed toward, this time caching the pipeline's final output rather than one intermediate step.
It skips the entire retrieve and generate pipeline when an identical request was already fully answered before.
2. Caching The End-To-End Result, Not Just One Stage
The embedding cache reuses just one intermediate step of the pipeline.
A response cache instead reuses the entire pipeline's final output at once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Cache type","What it reuses"],"rows":[["Embedding cache","One intermediate step, the computed vector"],["Response cache","The entire pipeline's final generated answer"]]}

blocks.text: 3. The Response Cache Key Must Include The Retrieved Context

blocks.alt: A query plus retrieved context forms the cache key

blocks.text: As with the cache key must include the model version in Embedding Cache, the same query against a changed knowledge base deserves a fresh answer, not the old cached one.
The cache key must reflect the retrieved context too, not just the raw query text.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A response cached purely by query text, would keep serving the old answer even after the underlying documents changed, unless the retrieved context itself is also part of the cache key.
blocks.text: A response cached purely by query text would keep serving the old answer even after the underlying documents changed, unless the retrieved context itself is also part of the cache key.
4. Response Cache Has The Biggest Latency Payoff

blocks.alt: Response cache skips everything while embedding cache skips one step

blocks.text: As with embedding cache reducing latency, not just cost, in Embedding Cache, skipping retrieval and generation both together saves far more time than skipping embedding alone.
Response caching is the single biggest latency win available in this module.
5. Response Caching Risks Surfacing Stale Answers

blocks.alt: A cached answer is compared against an updated knowledge base

blocks.text: A cached full answer can go stale the moment the underlying facts actually change.
Response caching carries the highest staleness risk of any cache in this pipeline.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Cache type","Staleness risk"],"rows":[["Embedding cache","Lower, invalidated by explicit model change"],["Response cache","Higher, tied to any change in underlying facts"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Time To Live As A Simple Invalidation Strategy

blocks.alt: A cached response has a time to live before it expires

blocks.text: As with invalidating the embedding cache on model change in Embedding Cache, a fixed expiration time bounds how long a stale cached answer can survive.
A simpler alternative to tracking every possible source of staleness individually.
7. Not All Responses Are Safe To Cache

blocks.alt: A static fact query is compared against a time-sensitive query

blocks.text: As with retrieving relevant memories, not all of them, in Memory, an answer personalized to one specific user should not be served to a different user from cache.
Response caching only applies safely to queries with a shared, user independent answer.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: An answer that references a specific user's account details, must never be cached and served to a different user, unlike a shared factual answer like a pricing question.
blocks.text: An answer that references a specific user's account details must never be cached and served to a different user, unlike a shared factual answer like a pricing question.
8. Layering Response Cache With Embedding Cache
A response cache miss can still hit the embedding cache underneath it.
The two caches stack, each catching what the other misses.
9. Recognizing When Response Caching Earns Its Staleness Risk

blocks.alt: High query repetition points toward using response caching

blocks.text: Frequently repeated, shared queries benefit most from response caching.
Rapidly changing or personalized queries should skip response caching entirely.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Caching a response by query text alone, ignoring changes to the underlying retrieved context.
Serving a cached response with no time-to-live, letting stale answers persist indefinitely.
Caching a personalized answer and serving it to a different user from the shared cache.
Treating the response cache and embedding cache as mutually exclusive instead of layered.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Response cache stores the complete generated answer for a given query and context.
Unlike an embedding cache, it reuses the pipeline's entire final output, not one intermediate step.
The cache key must reflect the retrieved context, not just the raw query text.
Response caching gives the biggest latency win, skipping both retrieval and generation on a hit.
Response caching carries the highest staleness risk, since a full answer can go outdated quickly.
A fixed time-to-live bounds how long a stale cached answer can survive.
Personalized answers must never be cached and served to a different user.
A response cache miss can still hit the embedding cache underneath it; the two caches stack.
